PMC Copyright notice PMCID: PMC12910625 NIHMSID: NIHMS2136118 PMID: 39251384 The publisher's version of this article is available at J Exp Anal Behav Abstract Cannabis demand is sensitive to next-day responsibilities, such as job interviews; however, it is unclear how demand is affected by non-work-related responsibilities and how reported compatibility of cannabis use (i.e., how suitable one perceives cannabis use to be in a situation) influences demand. This study examined the effects of a range of responsibilities on cannabis demand in a crowdsourced sample of adults who smoked cannabis at least monthly ( n = 177; 78% White; 47% women; mean age = 36.52). Participants completed hypothetical marijuana purchase tasks asking how much cannabis they would consume at escalating prices in the context of no responsibilities and next-day responsibilities spanning work, leisure, and caregiving. Cannabis demand was significantly reduced in all responsibility conditions ( p s < .008; d s .28–.94), with the largest reductions for the job interview and caring for children conditions. Higher ratings of suitability of cannabis use in each situation were correlated with higher demand. Finally, a qualitative thematic analysis characterized why cannabis use was considered suitable or unsuitable with each responsibility. These results suggest that demand is sensitive to next-day responsibilities. However, these effects are not uniform, and future research is needed to examine these individual differences and the timing of upcoming responsibilities. Keywords: behavioral economics, cannabis, demand, next-day responsibilities, reinforcement Cannabis remains the most used federally illicit drug in the United States, with as many as 22.0% of people aged 12 or older (i.e., 61.9 million people) consuming some form of cannabis in the past year ( Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration, 2023 ). Additionally, the U.S. policy landscape surrounding cannabis has significantly shifted in recent years, with 14 states and the District of Columbia legalizing cannabis for recreational use and 24 additional states legalizing cannabis for medical use as of January 2024. As access to legal cannabis for recreational and medical purposes continues to expand in the United States. and elsewhere, researchers must address factors underlying cannabis use and their broader impacts on public health and safety. Understanding factors contributing to increased cannabis use is necessary to improve prevention and intervention efforts. Behavioral economic researchers frame cannabis use as choice behavior sensitive to factors such as price, concurrently available alternatives, and delays to consumption ( Acuff, MacKillop, et al., 2023 ; Bickel et al., 2014 ). Consumption of any drug, including cannabis, fluctuates depending on the context in which the drug is obtained and consumed. The standard method that behavioral economists use to examine how drug preference and consumption change in response to specific contexts is through modified commodity purchase tasks. In the context of cannabis use, the marijuana purchase task (MPT; Aston et al., 2015 ; Collins et al., 2014 ) assesses cannabis demand (i.e., consumption in grams, joints, or hits as a function of price increases) in typical or specific drug-use situations. Consumption values are used to generate several demand indices, including intensity (i.e., consumption when the price is unconstrained), O max (i.e., maximum expenditure), P max (i.e., the price corresponding to O max ), and breakpoint (i.e., the price that suppresses consumption to zero). Demand curve modeling (e.g., Hursh & Silberberg, 2008 ; Koffarnus et al., 2015 ) is often used to derive an alpha parameter (α) reflecting the rate of change in elasticity as price increases. A recent meta-analysis of MPT studies found that greater cannabis demand is associated with greater consumption and severity of cannabis use disorder ( González-Roz et al., 2023 ). Thus, while there is robust support for the concurrent validity of the MPT, there is limited research examining contextual influences. One factor consistently shown to influence substance demand is the presence of a next-day responsibility. The premise is that drug and alcohol consumption is sensitive to the contingencies related to upcoming activities (e.g., having to work or attend class the next morning). In the first study to examine this topic, Skidmore and Murphy (2011) found that college students reported significantly lower alcohol demand when they had a test or class the next morning than when they had no specific obligations. These findings were later replicated and extended to other academic, family, and work-related responsibilities ( Gentile et al., 2012 ; Gilbert et al., 2014 ; Miller, Murphy, et al., 2023 ). Miller, Murphy, et al. (2023) expanded the range of responsibilities to include caregiving (e.g., caring for a child or another family member), leisure (e.g., going to the gym), or volunteering—in addition to work (e.g., having work or a job interview). Alcohol demand was attenuated in all responsibility conditions except for volunteering. While studies have assessed how different factors influence cannabis demand—such as social context ( Acuff, Strickland, et al., 2023 , cannabis cues ( Metrik et al., 2016 ; Miller et al., 2024 ), or cannabis strains ( Sholler et al., 2022 )—only two have examined the effect of next-day responsibilities on cannabis demand ( Acuff, Strickland,et al., 2023 ; Ferguson et al., 2021 ). Although it is reasonable to expect that next-day responsibilities would produce similar reductions in cannabis demand as observed for alcohol, there are a few reasons why cannabis demand may differ. The temporal duration of cannabis impairment generally is shorter than alcohol, and cannabis does not have the same hangover-like aftereffects as alcohol ( Huestis et al., 1992 ). Accordingly, it is important to examine how next-day responsibility contexts could impact cannabis use. In the first study addressing this question, Ferguson et al. (2021) had 186 crowdsourced adults who reported monthly or greater cannabis use complete MPTs with either a no-responsibility scenario or a next-day job interview scenario. Cannabis demand was more sensitive to price increases in the interview condition than in the no-responsibility condition, as indicated by significant reductions in intensity, breakpoint, and O max and increased α . Acuff, Strickland, et al. (2023) extended this line of research by examining the effect of opportunity cost—conceptualized as substantially greater work or school obligations than a typical week—on cannabis demand in a crowdsourced sample of adults who use cannabis. Demand was significantly lower in the high opportunity cost condition compared to a typical week. Though these results are informative, what remains unclear, is how other responsibilities beyond work or academic-related obligations influence cannabis demand. From a public health and policy perspective, understanding how cannabis demand, and by extension the level of cannabis use, is impacted by work, caregiving, or other personally relevant responsibilities has important implications for performance and safety in these roles. In addition, understanding these contextual influences is particularly relevant in the case of workplace drug testing (e.g., Mello, 2013 ; Phillips et al., 2015 ) and child safety and custody decisions (e.g., Lloyd & Brook, 2019 ). An additional component that may impact the effect of next-day responsibilities on cannabis demand is the extent to which people report those activities as incompatible with cannabis use. Researchers have added questions regarding the incompatibility, or unsuitability, of activities with alcohol use to activity surveys used in promoting alternative activity engagement to reduce hazardous alcohol use ( Weinsztok et al., 2023 ). Reporting activities to be more compatible with alcohol use and greater willingness to drink in incompatible situations is correlated with higher severity of alcohol misuse ( Weinsztok et al., 2023 ). Though these data are focused on alcohol demand, they may be relevant to cannabis demand in several ways. First, suitability levels can be used alongside MPTs as an additional metric to pinpoint the likelihood of cannabis use under varying contexts. Relatedly, measures of suitability have the potential to identify people most at risk for hazardous use. For example, when cannabis use may result in increased harm to oneself or others (e.g., when taking care of another person or working in a potentially dangerous setting), it can be helpful to pinpoint which people rate that activity to be compatible with use, as it can be an indicator of risky use patterns. This study aimed to replicate and extend Ferguson et al. (2021) by using a wider range of responsibilities and to explore how self-reported compatibility between cannabis use and responsibilities influences cannabis demand in these situations. We used a within-subjects design in which participants completed a hypothetical MPT with a no-responsibility vignette, followed by three to five responsibility MPTs (i.e., work, job interview, exercise, caring for kids, caring for another family member). We hypothesized that cannabis demand would be highest in the no-responsibility scenario, followed by the exercise scenario, and lowest in the work, interview, and caregiving scenarios. We also hypothesized that participants who reported cannabis use as less suitable with a given responsibility would report lower demand on the corresponding responsibility MPT. Finally, we conducted an exploratory qualitative analysis using an iterative thematic analysis approach to examine participants’ self-reported reasons for why cannabis use was considered suitable or unsuitable with each responsibility to contextualize further the relationship between responsibilities, suitability, and demand. Participants first completed a general screener with a few embedded cannabis-specific questions. We applied the following prescreen criteria in Prolific: (a) at least 18 years of age; (b) U.S. resident; (c) English fluency; (d) ≥ 95% approval rating; (e) ≥ 500 previous submissions. We then invited participants who reported monthly or greater cannabis use, reported smoking as their primary method of consuming cannabis (i.e., >50% of use), reported purchasing cannabis within the last year, and passed a multiple-choice attention check to participate in the second stage. Despite its significance, only one published replication exists. Recent studies link hindsight bias to depressive symptoms under memory design and emotionally relevant outcomes, but this has not been tested in a hypothetical design with neutral outcomes. This preregistered direct replication of Fischhoff’s Experiment 2 in a Brazilian sample (n = 431) explored associations with sociodemographic variables and depressive symptoms. We found no significant differences (p < 0.05) between retrospective and prospective judgments in our sample. No significant association (p < 0.05) was found between hindsight bias and depressive symptoms or other sociodemographic variables. An exploratory analysis found a small hindsight bias effect (d = 0.12; 95% CI [0.07; 0.37]). Although our study failed to replicate the original findings, a subsequent exploratory analysis revealed the presence of the phenomenon, albeit with a small effect size. These findings suggest low replicability of Fischhoff’s experiment with current modern techniques, and no association with depressive symptoms under hypothetical, neutral conditions. Keywords: Hindsight Bias, Depressive symptoms, Decision-Making, Replication, Open-Science HINDSIGHT BIAS: A PRE-REGISTERED REPLICATION-EXTENSION 3 Introduction Biases are one source of judgment errors, in which assessments are made based on expectations or experiences, causing a tendency to violate the normative rule, leading to suboptimal decisions (Rachlin, 1989). Among the several judgment biases previously documented (Kahneman et al., 1982), the hindsight bias has been thoroughly investigated in several domains of literature, such as business, law, and political sciences (Bernstein et al., 2016; Pezzo, 2011; Roese & Vohs, 2012). The phenomenon was established through the experiments conducted in the seminal article by Fischhoff (1975), revealing that judgments in hindsight (judgments made after an outcome is known) are overestimated compared to judgments in foresight (judgments made without knowing the outcome). Subsequent studies showed the robustness and pervasiveness of this phenomenon, being observed in most individuals, with a notable higher magnitude in preschoolers and the elderly (Bernstein et al., 2016; Groß & Bayen, 2015; Hoffrage & Pohl, 2003; Pezzo, 2011; Roese & Vohs, 2012). Also, evidence suggests that emotional mechanisms, particularly depression, play a role in hindsight bias (Groß et al., 2017; Groß & Bayen, 2017), which can potentially lead to the development of clinical approaches and guidelines. However, findings regarding its effect size, cross-cultural validity, and emotional/affect mechanisms are still mixed. We present a replication-extension study aimed to address such inconsistencies while providing updated information on the replicability of the experiments conducted by Fischhoff in 1975. 1. Fischhoff (1975) experiments The seminal study of Baruch Fischhoff (1975) is considered the first formal demonstration of hindsight bias (Bernstein et al., 2016; Pezzo, 2011; Roese & Vohs, 2012). The study has over 3.900 citations on Google Scholar by the time of this writing. It consisted of three experiments in which students were presented with four events in random order and asked to indicate the estimated probability for the occurrence of four possible outcomes described at the end of each event. For Experiment 1, students were randomized into one of 5 conditions: four After conditions (hindsight) and one Before condition (foresight). Participants in each of the After conditions were randomly given one of the four possible outcomes as the "true ending" (one After condition per outcome), while participants in the Before condition did not. Experiment 2 included the condition After (ignore), which had the same procedures and stimulus as the After condition (thus, also divided into four conditions), with the addition of asking the participants to respond “as they would have had they not known the outcome”. Finally, Experiment 3 repeated the same procedures as Experiment 1, but asked the participants to respond “as had other student judges who had not known the true outcome”, in conditions named Before (others) and After (others). The results from HINDSIGHT BIAS: A PRE-REGISTERED REPLICATION-EXTENSION 4 these three experiments showed that: Experiment 1 - outcome knowledge affects judgments, as participants in the After conditions overestimated the probability for the outcome given, regardless of which; Experiment 2 - people are either unaware of this effect or cannot ignore it, as participants in the After (ignore) condition overestimated what they would have known without outcome knowledge; and Experiment 3 - people also overestimate what others would have predicted without outcome knowledge, as participants in After (others) condition showed similar patterns compared to After (ignore) condition. 2. Hindsight bias The hindsight bias is a tendency to overestimate judgments of an uncertain event once its outcome is revealed. As such, having prior knowledge of an event’s outcome increases the perceived likelihood of its occurrence, leading people to overestimate what was known and what would have been known at the time when the outcome was uncertain (Fischhoff, 1975; Fischhoff & Beyth, 1975; Groß & Bayen, 2015; Pezzo & Beckstead, 2008; Roese & Vohs, 2012). The most comprehensive theoretical model currently encompasses a three-level structure of hindsight bias, starting from basic memory processes and climbing up to self-inferential beliefs (Bernstein et al., 2016; Roese & Vohs, 2012). The first level is memory distortion, manifested by the misrecollection of past judgments (e.g., “I said it would happen”). Second, is the inevitability level, in which beliefs of the causality of events make an outcome seem more predictable, predetermined, or inevitable (e.g., “It had to happen”). The third and last level is foreseeability, where a person’s beliefs about their prediction capabilities lead to an impression that they could have foreseen the outcome of an event (e.g., “I knew it would happen”) (Bernstein et al., 2016; Roese & Vohs, 2012). Figure S1 in the supplementary materials depicts this model's visual summary. This phenomenon is associated with negative consequences for behaviour and emotions, causing impacts on several domains of society, such as legal decisions and medical diagnoses (Louie et al., 2007; Roese & Vohs, 2012). Two main consequences are attributed to hindsight bias: myopia - higher attributions of negligence and blame due to focusing on a single causal explanation while disregarding others; and overconfidence - unjustified certainty in predictions, inflating oneself’s capacity of assessment and leading to riskier decisions (Bernstein et al., 2016; LaBine & LaBine, 1996; Roese & Vohs, 2012). Generally, the hindsight bias is measured by comparing foresight and hindsight judgments, which can be obtained by asking the participant to estimate the correct value for an uncertain quantity, the probability of an event’s outcome, or whether a given statement is true or false (Pezzo, 2011; Pohl, 2007). When judgments are made without knowledge of the correct answer, they are considered foresight judgments. On the other hand, judgments made after receiving information on the correct answer are considered “hindsight” HINDSIGHT BIAS: A PRE-REGISTERED REPLICATION-EXTENSION 5 judgments. There are two main experimental designs, each capturing the hindsight bias at different levels (Bernstein et al., 2016; Pohl, 2007; Roese & Vohs, 2012). The memory design is a within-subject design in which participants first respond to a set of tasks, where the hindsight judgment is obtained by providing feedback on the correct answer and asking participants to recall their original answers as accurately as possible, disregarding the feedback. This design is best for capturing both the memory distortion and the inevitability level of hindsight bias. The hypothetical design is a between-subject design, in which both groups are asked to make a judgment, most commonly by estimating the probability of different outcomes of a short story. The hindsight judgment is obtained by providing feedback on the correct answer before the judgment task and asking participants to respond to what they would have answered if they had not received the feedback (thus, a hypothetical judgment). This was the design used in the experiments of Fischhoff (1975), which is capable of apprehending more complex processes of the mind (Roese & Vohs, 2012), argued to be more adequate to measure judgments at the foreseeability and inevitability levels (Giroux et al., 2023). The current consensus is that the hindsight bias is a pervasive and robust phenomenon, consistently observed in several real-world situations (Roese and Vohs 2012; Pezzo 2011). Noteworthy, studies have consistently shown that hindsight bias tends to be stronger in older adults and children, following a U-shaped pattern across the life span (Bernstein et al. 2011; Coolin et al. 2014; Groß and Bayen 2015; Pohl et al. 2018). Studies suggested that the age-related differences in recall ability and inhibitory control may account for this phenomenon (Groß and Bayen 2015). 2.1. Hindsight Bias and Depression Major depressive disorder is a mental disorder characterised by a persistent pattern of sad, unhappy, or irritable mood, as well as distress and impairment in various areas of life (American Psychiatric Association, 2022). It is estimated that 185 million people have this disorder, with a 12-month prevalence of 4 to 5%, affecting women twice as high as men, and with a prevalence in individuals aged 18 to 29 years three times higher than the prevalence in individuals over 60 years (American Psychiatric Association, 2022; Marx et al., 2023). Its symptomatic manifestations are feelings of guilt, ruminations about the past, an exaggerated sense of responsibility for adversities, misinterpretation of neutral everyday events, and cognitive problems, such as impaired decision-making and reduced thinking and concentration skills (American Psychiatric Association, 2022). The cognitive problems inherent in depression tend to be persistent and recurrent (Chamberlain & Sahakian, 2004), manifested as a negative bias towards aspects of the environment (Noworyta et al., 2021), such as greater recall of negative than positive HINDSIGHT BIAS: A PRE-REGISTERED REPLICATION-EXTENSION 6 memories (Brittlebank et al., 1993). People with depression manifest a pessimistic judgment bias (Douglas & Porter, 2010; Maniglio et al., 2014), that is, an overestimation of negative events (Carver & Scheier, 2014), as well as a hypersensitivity to negative feedback (Spasojević & Alloy, 2001) and also a hyposensitivity to positive feedback (Henriques et al., 1994; McFarland & Klein, 2009; Noworyta et al., 2021; Robinson et al., 2012). Considering the cognitive components of depression and its affective impact through a bias of pessimistic judgment, ruminations of the past, attributions of guilt, and an exaggerated sense of responsibility. These cognitive aspects of depression closely align with the emotional mechanisms of hindsight bias. A study from Haslam and Jayasinghe (1995) found that dysphoria was associated with hindsight bias in students' grade predictions, influenced by initial optimism or pessimism, thus suggesting a role of motivational or affective factors. A study by Groß and Bayen (2017) investigated hindsight bias in a sample of nondysphoric participants with induced negative mood and dysphoric participants and found that, while both groups showed hindsight bias when recalling answers to difficult questions, dysphoria was associated with a stronger reconstruction bias, and recollection bias was present only in a neutral mood but absent in dysphoric or induced negative mood. In a subsequent study by both authors in 2021, two groups of younger and older adults rated the foreseeability and inevitability of everyday-life scenarios that could end with a positive or a negative outcome. The study revealed that, although both groups did not differ in their impressions of inevitability or foreseeability of outcomes, older adults showed a stronger memory component of hindsight bias than younger adults, especially after negative outcomes (Groß & Bayen, 2021). Most notably, a "depressive hindsight bias" was suggested by Groß et al. (2017). Their study revealed that, after listening to (and imagining themselves in) everyday scenarios that could end with a positive or a negative outcome, participants with higher levels of depression showed a stronger hindsight bias for negative outcomes, judging them as more foreseeable and inevitable, and also misremembering prior expectations as more negative. Notably, all of the aforementioned studies investigated the hindsight bias using the memory design and emotionally relevant outcomes. To our knowledge, there is no study on depressive symptoms and hindsight bias under the hypothetical design or with neutral outcomes. Further understanding the implications of hindsight bias on depressive symptoms may help lead to the development of clinical approaches and guidelines for this population. 3. Abstract: Leib et al. (2024) examine how artificial intelligence (AI) generated advice affects dishonesty compared to equivalent human advice in a laboratory experiment. In their preferred empirical specification, the authors report that dishonesty-promoting advice increases dishonest behavior by approximately 15% compared to a baseline without advice, while honesty-promoting advice has no significant effect. Additionally, they find that algorithmic transparency - disclosing whether advice comes from AI or humans - does not affect behavior. We computationally reproduce the main results of the paper using the same procedures and original data. Our results confirm the sign, magnitude, and statistical significance of the authors' reported estimates across each of their main findings. Robert Reed ( University of Canterbury ) Registered: W. Robert Reed Abstract This study critically examines the reproducibility and robustness of Stanley et al. (2023). Stanley et al. analyzed 67,308 meta-analysis datasets from the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews (CDSR). They find that a generalized Fixed Effect estimator they call unrestricted weighted least squares (UWLS-FE) is determined by the model selection criteria AIC and BIC to be superior to Random Effects (RE). In some cases, it is also better than Fixed Effects. Our analysis uses their original data and code and exactly reproduces their results. However, we show that the small sample sizes of the CDSR datasets undermine the reliability of AIC and BIC for model selection. Accordingly, we simulate 108,000 datasets mirroring the original CDSR data. This allows us to know the true model parameters and evaluate the estimators more accurately. Our findings suggest that RE generally outperforms UWLS-FE. The comparison with FE is less clear. FE frequently produces more accurate standard errors than UWLS-FE, making confidence intervals and hypothesis testing more reliable. However, for some types of data, UWLS-FE may be better than FE. In a landmark longitudinal study, Brod, Bunge, and Shing (2017) followed children around the transition to first grade and found that those who entered formal schooling showed greater improvements in cognitive control and greater increases in right parietal brain activation over one year than same- aged children who remained in a play-based kindergarten. We confirm the key findings: first graders improved more than kindergartners on an EF task (the Hearts and Flowers task), especially in trials requiring cognitive control, and only first graders showed a significant increase in right posterior parietal cortex activation during an independent go/no-go task. Extension analyses revealed no significant effects of child gender or cohort on outcomes. We also found that changes in dorsolateral prefrontal cortex activation did not significantly correlate with performance changes, underscoring the specific role of PPC. Our findings confirm that formal schooling enhances children’s cognitive control beyond age effects, as indicated by greater improvements in task accuracy and heightened PPC recruitment, and we discuss new insights regarding moderating factors and brain-behavior relationships. REPLICATION AND EXTENSION OF SCHOOLING EFFECTS ON CHILDREN'S COGNITIVE CONTROL 3 Introduction During early childhood, children undergo a “5-to-7-year shift,” characterized by remarkable improvements in executive functions (EF) such as attention regulation, inhibitory control, and cognitive flexibility. This developmental leap raises questions about the underlying drivers: to what extent are gains in EF simply a product of brain maturation versus the influence of new environmental demands like formal schooling? Prior research offers mixed insights. On one hand, age-related neural development undoubtedly contributes to EF improvements (Durston et al., 2002). On the other hand, schooling may catalyze EF growth by providing structured activities that challenge cognitive control (Burrage et al., 2011; Morrison et al., 2011). For example, a natural experiment by Burrage et al. (2008) found that children who transitioned to formal schooling showed greater EF gains than those who remained in informal settings of the same age. Similarly, Weiland and Yoshikawa (2013) demonstrated that attending an academically oriented pre-kindergarten program led to improvements in inhibitory control and attention in 4-year-olds. These studies suggest that the school context – with its emphasis on rule-based learning and attention maintenance – can accelerate EF development. Neurodevelopmental findings further implicate specific brain networks in EF improvements. The frontoparietal attention network, including the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC) and posterior parietal cortex (PPC), plays a key role in goal-directed attention and cognitive control. Corbetta and Shulman (2002) highlighted that the PPC, in particular, is involved in directing top-down attention. In children, increased activation of these regions is associated with better inhibitory control and working memory (Durston et al., 2002; Davidson et al., 2006). It follows that age or schooling-related EF gains may be reflected in heightened engagement of frontoparietal regions. However, it is unclear whether schooling uniquely alters brain activation above and beyond maturation. To disentangle these factors, Brod, Bunge, and Shing (2017) conducted a longitudinal REPLICATION AND EXTENSION OF SCHOOLING EFFECTS ON CHILDREN'S COGNITIVE CONTROL 4 study leveraging a school-entry cutoff. They followed children of about 5 years old born just before vs. after the enrollment cutoff for first grade. Crucially, at baseline the two groups were of comparable age; over the next year, one group experienced formal schooling (first grade) while the other remained in kindergarten (play-oriented, less formal academics). This design aimed to isolate the impact of one year of schooling on EF improvements and brain changes. Brod et al. assessed cognitive control behaviorally using two tasks and measured brain activation with functional MRI (fMRI) during an EF task. They reported that first graders (“school” group) showed larger gains in EF task accuracy over the year than kindergartners. Furthermore, fMRI revealed greater increases in right PPC activation for first graders relative to kindergartners during an attention-demanding task, and this neural change correlated with performance improvements. These findings indicate that formal schooling can amplify EF development and that such benefits are mirrored in specific brain activation patterns. The present work aims to replicate and extend the study by Brod et al. (2017). Replication is critical for validating influential findings on schooling effects, especially given their implications for education policy and developmental theory. Using the original dataset made available by the authors, we reproduce the key behavioral and neuroimaging analyses. This includes mixed-design ANOVAs on task performance (accuracy and reaction time) and ROI- based ANOVAs on fMRI percent signal change in frontal and parietal regions. By successfully replicating these results, we can confirm the robustness of the conclusions that one year of schooling measurably boosts cognitive control abilities and alters brain function in young children. Beyond replication, we introduce new analyses to deepen understanding of these effects. First, we examine potential moderating factors such as gender and cohort (wave). Brod et al. noted that child gender and cohort did not significantly influence results, but they did not report detailed statistics. We formally test interactions involving gender (e.g., whether boys vs. girls REPLICATION AND EXTENSION OF SCHOOLING EFFECTS ON CHILDREN'S COGNITIVE CONTROL 5 benefit differently from schooling) and cohort (whether the pattern held across two data- collection waves). Second, we explore additional brain-behavior relationships. The original study found a significant correlation between PPC activation change and EF improvement. We extend this by assessing whether changes in the dlPFC – another region implicated in cognitive control – also relate to performance gains. If schooling broadly enhances frontoparietal engagement, one might expect parallel changes in dlPFC; however, if the effect is specific to parietal attention networks, dlPFC changes may be less behaviorally relevant. Finally, we perform subgroup analyses of EF improvement (e.g., comparing initial vs. final performance distributions) to characterize the longitudinal trends in more detail. For instance, we test whether the schooling group improved particularly on the more challenging task conditions (incongruent and mixed trials) – a point alluded to but not deeply examined in the original paper. In summary, our study not only verifies the findings of Brod et al. (2017) but also extends them to address additional questions. This comprehensive approach provides greater insight into how formal education contributes to cognitive development and its neural underpinnings during a critical period of childhood. Small View a PDF of the paper titled Exploration, Confirmation, and Replication in the Same Observational Study: A Two Team Cross-Screening Approach to Studying the Effect of Unwanted Pregnancy on Mothers' Later Life Outcomes, by Samrat Roy and 5 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: The long term consequences of unwanted pregnancies carried to term on mothers have not been much explored. We use data from the Wisconsin Longitudinal Study (WLS) and propose a novel approach, namely two team cross-screening, to study the possible effects of unwanted pregnancies carried to term on various aspects of mothers' later-life mental health, physical health, economic well-being and life satisfaction. Our method, unlike existing approaches to observational studies, enables the investigators to perform exploratory data analysis, confirmatory data analysis and replication in the same study. This is a valuable property when there is only a single data set available with unique strengths to perform exploratory, confirmatory and replication analysis. In two team cross-screening, the investigators split themselves into two teams and the data is split as well according to a meaningful covariate. Each team then performs exploratory data analysis on its part of the data to design an analysis plan for the other part of the data. The complete freedom of the teams in designing the analysis has the potential to generate new unanticipated hypotheses in addition to a prefixed set of hypotheses. However, the coexistence of socially progressive attitudes and more conservative economic tendencies within this class deserves more scrutiny among political scientists because such tendencies, I argue, may reveal differences of consequence for electoral and policy outcomes. More specifically, I point to two analytical blindspots in research on progressive politics: the separation of socio-cultural and economic issues, which can conceal critical policy preferences within the knowledge economy class, and the prevailing dichotomy of knowledge economy ‘winners’ and ‘losers’, which can underestimate the potential for status concerns in the knowledge economy class. We use time pressure to capture intuitive decision making and a dictator game to measure prosocial behavior. We also estimate and test for “population heterogeneity” in the effect size. First, we exogenously vary subject experience with economic games to test whether experience influences the treatment effect. Second, we leverage our data structure to conduct a "pseudo meta-analysis," assessing effect size heterogeneity across several potential sources of heterogeneity. This helps us assess whether prior findings in the literature stem from false positives or genuine heterogeneity in effect sizes. Our results show no evidence that experience with economic experiments moderates the time pressure effect. Further, the estimated heterogeneity in effect sizes in the pseudo meta- analysis is negligible, we cannot reject the null hypothesis of a uniform p-value distribution, and our rejection rate aligns with the expected 5% from chance alone. These findings support the view that the apparent link between prosocial behavior and intuitive processing is likely due to false positives rather than heterogeneous treatment effects. Introduction When a replication study fails, a common explanation is that the treatment effect is heterogenous – it varies across individuals and contexts – and that the background conditions of the replication study were different to those present in the original study. When effect sizes are heterogeneous, this explanation is both reasonable and accurate. However, as statistically significant effects are more likely to be reported and published, a research literature could end up consisting of a pattern of mixed findings resembling heterogeneous effects even if there is no genuine heterogeneity. In such cases, a mixed pattern of findings is better explained as a result of false positives being published alongside null findings. It is difficult to distinguish between these two competing explanations as both account for a mixed pattern of findings. An example of a large research literature where several replication failures have been attributed to heterogeneous treatment effects is the literature on the “Social Heuristics Hypothesis” (SHH), originally formulated by Rand, Greene & Nowak (2012) and Rand et al. (2014) and formalized in Bear & Rand (2016). This hypothesis posits that intuition employs heuristics evolved in everyday experience where prosocial behavior is typically advantageous, but that reflection tunes behavior to the one-shot setting in the lab and therefore leads to more selfish decisions. Several studies failed to replicate the original findings in favor of the SHH (e.g., Tinghög et al., 2013; Camerer et al., 2018), including a many-lab direct replication study (Bouwmeester et al., 2017) that found no effect consistently across laboratories. A meta-analysis by Rand (2016) found evidence for an overall intuitive cooperation effect across studies and a meta-analysis by Rand et al. (2016) suggested an effect of intuitive decision making on dictator game giving among women. Other meta-analyses point in the opposite direction; Kvarven et al. (2020) suggest that there is no intuitive cooperation effect and Fromell, Nosenzo & Owens (2020) reach similar conclusions regarding the dictator game. Other studies that have found a link between intuition and cooperation or prosocial behavior include Døssing, Piovesan & Engström (2017), Everett et al. (2017), Rand, Greene & Nowak (2012) and Schulz et al. (2014). Studies finding no effect include Verkoejen & Bouwmeester (2014), Hauge et al. (2016), Merkel & Lohse (2018); Tinghög et al. (2016). Other studies in this literature include Isler et al. (2021) and Isler, Yilmaz & Maule (2021). The literature is largely divided between those who believe that the mixed pattern of findings can be explained by the fact that the intuitive prosociality is heterogeneous across individuals and contexts (e.g., Rand, 2016; Shi et al. 2020), and those who argue that there is no clear relationship between intuition and prosocial behavior (e.g., Kvarven et al., 2020; Fromell, Nosenzo & Owens, 2020). In this paper, we will refer to the former as the “heterogeneity hypothesis” and the latter as the “false positive hypothesis”. Examples of explanations in line with the “heterogeneity hypothesis” are Alós-Ferrer & Garagnani (2020), Chen & Krajbich (2018); Rand et al. (2014), Rand (2018), McAuliffe et al. (2018), Strømland, Tjøtta & Torsvik (2016) and Goeschl & Lohse (2018). In this paper, we use a combination of a lab experiment and meta-analytic approaches to try to distinguish between these two competing hypotheses. We conduct a 2 x 2 lab experiment in the Norwegian Citizen Panel, a survey data set constructed to be representative of the general Norwegian population on observable characteristics. We collected a sample of 1390 individuals. We exogenously vary a time constraint (time pressure vs time delay) and whether subjects have previous experience with economics experiments. This is done by randomly assigning about half of the participants into a standard Dictator game prior to participating in the Dictator game with time constraints. Previous studies have suggested based on correlational evidence that experience undermines the effect of intuition manipulations and that the SHH predicts this pattern as experienced subjects may have already adapted their heuristics to the situation (Rand et al., 2014). This explanation was also used by Rand (2018) to explain a replication failure by Camerer et al. (2018). Another reason to study the causal effect of experience on the time pressure effect is that experience seems to be negatively correlated with treatment effects in general (Chandler et al., 2015). We further exploit the structure of our data and use meta-analytic methods applied to our data set to try to distinguish between the two competing explanations proposed in the literature. This analysis is motivated by various suggestions by methodologists to do statistical inferences on a distribution of effects rather than single results (e.g., Leamer, 1983; Sala-I-Martin, 1997; Simonsohn, Simmons & Nelson, 2020; Steegen et al., 2016). The main idea behind our approach is that the “heterogeneity hypothesis” and “false positive hypothesis” imply a distinct pattern of results across different model specifications within the same data set. If there is no underlying effect and no heterogeneity, one would expect a distribution of effect sizes centered around zero with little estimated heterogeneity (using meta-analytic approaches) and a uniform distribution of p-values across model specifications with a rejection rate close to 5%. But if there is an underlying effect or the effect is highly heterogeneous, one would expect a non-uniform distribution of p-values with a rejection rate higher than the nominal rate, and that meta-analytic methods applied to the full range of estimated models would suggest sizable heterogeneity. Our findings, both from the lab experiment and “pseudo meta-analysis” (meta-analysis methods applied to a single data set) are more consistent with the false positive hypothesis than the heterogeneity hypothesis. They are also consistent with a theoretical model by Maniadis, Tufano & List (2014; 2017) who builds on Ioannidis (2005). This model suggests that an increase in researcher degrees of freedom – the number of possible statistical tests that can be used to support a given research hypothesis – lowers the post-study probability (PSP) that a randomly chosen statistically significant test is true. The model suggests that literatures where the research hypothesis is frequently (or primarily) supported by significant subgroup tests are more likely to contain false positive findings. This paper proceeds as follows. Section 2 presents the two competing hypotheses to be considered. Section 3 outlines the data and experimental design. Section 4 features our data analysis, and section 5 concludes the paper. 2. Two competing hypotheses There are several potential sources of heterogeneity in an effect size of interest. We can distinguish between population heterogeneity, design heterogeneity and analytical heterogeneity (Holzmeister et al., 2024). Population heterogeneity is present if the effect differs across different populations for the same design and analysis choices. Design heterogeneity is present if the effect size varies by the experimental design, for a given population and analysis. Analytical heterogeneity is present if the analysis path implemented by the researcher influences the effect size, holding the population and experimental design fixed. In our study, the experimental design is fixed, and the same analyst is doing all the analysis which means that we are only able to address population heterogeneity, however, we will be able to do this in a clean way. When doing a conventional meta-analysis of the published literature, it is difficult to distinguish between the three potential sources of heterogeneity in the effect size because studies making up a meta-analysis differ in analytical approach, the population that the study is drawn from and the experimental design details. How could a pattern of apparently heterogeneous treatment effects instead be due to false positives? Following Ioannidis (2005), consider the “post-study probability” (PSP), the probability that a randomly drawn research finding in a literature is true, conditional on being statistically significant, 𝑃𝑆𝑃= (1 −𝛽)𝜋+ 𝛽𝜋𝑢 (1 −𝛽)𝜋+ 𝛽𝜋𝑢+ [𝛼+ (1 −𝛼)𝑢](1 −𝜋) Here, 𝜋 is the prior probability that the claim is true, (1 −𝛽) is the statistical power, 𝛼 is the significance level and 𝑢 captures the extent to which research findings in the literature are biased through some form of selective reporting. For instance, with 20 binary choices we have over a million possible ways to analyze the same data set (Ioannidis, 2018). In literatures where it is not deemed acceptable to appeal to subgroup analyses – that is, the only finding that will be seen as consistent with the underlying research hypothesis is a statistically significant finding in the main sample – the degrees of freedom available to the researcher are inevitably smaller than in a literature where a statistically significant finding in either of a large number of subgroups will be sufficient to see the overall research hypothesis as supported. However, the two hypotheses make distinct predictions about the results one would expect in a number of different data sets in absence of selective reporting or publication bias. When the null is universally true and there is no heterogeneity, the distribution of p-values is uniform on the [0, 1] interval (e.g., Hung et al., 1997). If we split the sample into subsamples and perform statistical tests we should therefore, according to the “false positive hypothesis”, expect a uniform distribution of p-values and a rejection rate equal to the nominal rate 𝛼. However, when there is heterogeneity in the effect size this is no longer true and we should expect a higher rejection rate than the nominal rate (Holzmeister et al., 2024) and a non-uniform distribution of p-values. The problem with testing the above predictions using the published literature is that we cannot rule out selective reporting (e.g., publication bias or ”p-hacking”) of statistically significant findings. These mechanisms lead to a higher rejection rate even when the null is true (Simonsohn, Nelson & Simmons, 2014). Further, as published studies can differ both on design features, population features and the chosen analytical path, it is hard to know whether the proposed source of heterogeneity in a published study is the actual source of heterogeneity in the effect size. In our data set, we have access to a relatively large sample of individuals (N = 1390) sampled from the general Norwegian population and we have access to a decent amount of background information on these individuals. Recent research on this phenomenon has oscillated between simulation studies, probability calculations based on hypothetical voter preferences, and empirical analyses often limited by unsatisfactory data. This paper presents the first comprehensive evaluation of 253 electoral polls conducted across 59 countries. Our findings demonstrate that the Condorcet paradox has virtually no empirical relevance: with only one exception, we find no evidence of cyclical majorities in any of the 253 elections. This result remains robust after statistical inference testing. Furthermore, this study provides insights into which parties are particularly likely to emerge as Condorcet winners and explores how these Condorcet winners assert themselves after elections. Keywords: Elections; Condorcet Paradox; Condorcet Winner; Voting JEL-Code: D71 1 1. Introduction The ideal of democracy demands that collective decisions reflect majority judg- ments. An alternative x should be chosen over y if more voters prefer x to y. A Condorcet winner—an alternative that de- feats all other contestants in pairwise ma- jority comparisons—has intuitive appeal as it aligns with the principle of majority de- cision (Sen, 2017, Ch. 5). However, such a winner may not exist. Even when voters have transitive preferences, majority am- algamation can produce intransitive out- comes, a phenomenon known as the Con- dorcet paradox (Condorcet, 1785, p. lxj (76)). A simple example involves three voters and three candidates: Voter 1 ranks A ≻B ≻C, Voter 2 ranks B ≻C ≻A, and Voter 3 ranks C ≻A ≻B. Here, A beats B by majority, B beats C, and C beats A, violating transitivity. The Condorcet paradox, intensely de- bated during the French Revolution, faded into obscurity for nearly 150 years (Roth- schild, 2005; McLean, 2019, p. 99) be- fore Arrow’s groundbreaking impossibility theorem revived its significance. Arrow (1950) demonstrated that adherence to ma- jority principles risks indeterminate out- comes, whereas ensuring decisiveness re- quires abandoning the majority principle and possibly accepting a majority-defeated winner. Beyond the confines of voting the- ory, the Condorcet paradox highlights a fundamental challenge to (economic) core stability (Moulin, 2014). Despite its theoretical significance, the empirical relevance of the paradox in demo- cratic elections remains insufficiently sub- stantiated. The most recent survey con- cluded that its empirical relevance is far from settled (Van Deemen, 2013), largely due to a persistent lack of reliable data. Most results on the occurrence of Con- dorcet paradoxes are based on simulated data (Lepelley and Martin, 2001; Gehr- lein, 2006; Sauermann, 2022), or on non- political elections, like electing the head of an academic association (Chamberlin et al., 1984; Feld and Grofman, 1992; Regenwet- ter et al., 2007; Tideman, 2009; Popov et al., 2014). Empirical studies of real-world (demo- cratic) elections are scarce. Many contributions investigate primary elec- tions (Kurrild-Klitgaard, 2018), referenda (Bochsler, 2010; Justesen, 2007), or sub- national elections (Munkøe, 2014; Dar- mann and Klamler, 2023). Studies of national parliamentary elections are only available for three countries: Iran 2017 (Feizi et al., 2020), the UK in 2010 (Ab- ramson et al., 2013), and Denmark 1973- 2005 (Van Deemen and Vergunst, 1998; Kurrild-Klitgaard, 2001, 2008). Empirical studies on presidential elections are limited to the US (Riker, 1988; Abramson et al., 1995; Potthoff and Munger, 2021), and France in 2007 (Abramson, 2007). Only one empirical study investigates the (non- )occurrence of the Condorcet Paradox com- paratively for 12 West European countries in 2004, but there data was not collected in the context of national elections (Mc- Donald et al., 2012). Based on the liter- ature, two elections likely revealed the ex- istence of a Condordet Paradox: the 2016 US election (Potthoff and Munger, 2021), and the Danish election in 1994 (Kurrild- Klitgaard, 2008). This evidence is far too limited to evaluate the empirical relevance of the Condorcet Paradox in real-world na- tional elections, especially considering elec- tions in non-Western democracies. Adding to the challenge is the observa- tion that most studies refrain from mak- ing claims about statistical inference. (2019), with the latter two explicitly assess- ing the robustness of their findings through bootstrap methods. Eminent economists have recently ad- vocated for electoral reforms in favour of the Condorcet method, even beyond the academic realm (Maskin and Sen, 2016, 2017b,a). In this public discourse, the Con- dorcet paradox is the unresolved core issue, as it is – alongside the debate over whether cardinal information should be considered – the main argument against the practical implementation of the Condorcet method. Sen (2017, Ch. 10.2) highlighted the ne- cessity of determining the relevance of the Condorcet paradox through a comprehens- ive empirical analysis as a basis for ad- vancing discussions on electoral reforms. Such a study should ideally cover various points in time and different societies. Mo- tivated by this research desideratum, our work presents a comprehensive study that examines the occurrence of the Condorcet paradox across numerous elections, span- ning multiple countries and time periods. We analyse data from 253 elections across 59 countries provided by the Comparative Study of Electoral Systems (CSES, 2024). Our findings indicate that the Condorcet paradox has virtually no em- pirical relevance, a conclusion that remains robust even after accounting for statistical inference. Beyond this, we provide insights into who the Condorcet winners are and eval- uate the extent to which different electoral systems succeed in bringing these winners to office (in candidate elections) or into government (in parliamentary elections). We also examine which parties, identified as Condorcet winners, fail to win elections. Thus, for the first time, we offer insight into the identification and success of Condorcet winners. 2. Today the circulation of knowledge in science is restricted by high prices. Many students and researchers cannot afford academic journals and books that are locked behind paywalls. Sci-Hub emerged in 2011 to tackle this problem. Since then, the website has revolutionized the way science is being done. Sci-Hub is helping millions of students and researchers, medical professionals, journalists and curious people in all countries to unlock access to knowledge. The mission of Sci-Hub is to fight every obstacle that prevents open access to knowledge: be it legal, technical or otherwise.
